note.claim: Luther's challenge split the Empire into confessional camps that no imperial institution could arbitrate, which removed the one thing that had kept princely quarrels from becoming a general war.
note.objection: The war's immediate causes were Habsburg ambition in Bohemia and a succession fight; confessional lines were crossed on both sides, with Catholic France paying Protestant Sweden.
note.warrant: When the institution that arbitrated disputes loses its authority, the next dispute becomes a war.
note.verdict: Necessary, high confidence. Without the confessional split there is a Habsburg succession war in Bohemia, as in 1546 and 1552, and it stays regional; the thirty years and the foreign armies required the religious frame that made every prince's choice a matter for every other prince.

tests.hoop: Every major belligerent declared a confessional reason for entering (passed)
tests.gun: None: no document shows the war impossible without the split

note.claim: The Peace of Augsburg was a direct settlement of the split Luther caused: each prince chose his territory's religion because the Empire could no longer impose one.
note.objection: Augsburg also answered the Schmalkaldic War and Charles V's failure to crush the Protestant princes by force in 1547-52; the military stalemate, not the theology, produced the formula.
note.warrant: A settlement that ratifies a stalemate lasts as long as the stalemate.
note.verdict: Sufficient, high confidence. The split produced the war and the war produced the formula; no other input is needed to explain the settlement's content, which is cuius regio, eius religio.

note.claim: Augsburg's silence on Calvinism and its unclear rule on church lands secularised after 1552 left two fault lines that the 1618 crisis ran along.
note.objection: The settlement held for sixty-three years, longer than most; the war began in Bohemia over a Habsburg king's revocation of Protestant rights, which Augsburg did not cover at all.
note.warrant: A settlement's gaps decide the shape of the next conflict, not whether it comes.
note.verdict: Contributing, moderate confidence. The set: Habsburg ambition under Ferdinand II (ranks first), the Bohemian estates' election of a Calvinist king (second), Augsburg's gaps (third), Spanish strategic interest in the Rhine corridor (fourth).

note.claim: Thirty years of war that killed perhaps a third of the German population produced a settlement because every party was exhausted and none could win.
note.objection: The settlement's terms, especially sovereignty for the princes and the French and Swedish guarantees, reflected who was winning in 1648 as much as exhaustion; a decisive victory would have produced a different peace.
note.warrant: Exhaustion produces a peace; the balance of forces at the end writes its terms.
note.verdict: Sufficient, high confidence. The war is enough to explain that a settlement came; the terms needed the particular stalemate of 1645-48.

note.claim: Westphalia fixed German fragmentation in law, giving some 300 territories rights of alliance and war, so that the Empire survived as a frame and ceased to be a state.
note.objection: The Empire functioned for another 158 years, with courts, diets and a working constitution; it was Napoleon's armies and the Confederation of the Rhine that ended it, and he could have kept it as a client.
note.warrant: A constitution that guarantees its parts against its centre survives until an outside power finds the parts useful.
note.verdict: Contributing, moderate confidence. The set: Napoleon's decision to reorganise the German states as French clients (ranks first), the Habsburgs' prior decision to found an Austrian Empire in 1804 (second), Westphalian fragmentation (third).

note.claim: The Westphalian settlement is cited as the origin of the sovereign-state system that the UN Charter codified in 1945, in Article 2's rule of non-intervention.
note.objection: Osiander (2001) and Croxton (1999) show the 1648 treaties say almost nothing about sovereignty and much about imperial law; the 'Westphalian system' is a reading constructed by nineteenth-century jurists and twentieth-century political scientists.
note.warrant: A founding myth can be more consequential than the founding, once institutions act on it.
note.verdict: Contested, low confidence. The realist school treats 1648 as the hinge; the revisionists treat it as a label applied later. The link is kept because the Charter's drafters believed the myth, which is a cause of a different kind.

note.claim: Frederick's seizure of Silesia made Prussia a great power and created the Austro-Prussian dualism that had to be resolved before Germany could be united under either.
note.objection: A century and a quarter separate the two; Prussia nearly ceased to exist in 1806-07, and the dualism was resolved by the war of 1866, which Bismarck chose and could have lost.
note.warrant: A rivalry between two candidates for the same role is settled by whichever first finds a war it can win.
note.verdict: Contributing, high confidence. The set: Bismarck's wars of 1864-71 (ranks first), the Zollverein's economic facts (second), the dualism from 1740 (third), the failure of 1848 (fourth).

note.claim: The Congress of Vienna had to fill the void Napoleon left in Germany, and did so with the German Confederation of 39 states under an Austrian presidency.
note.objection: Vienna settled all of Europe, not only Germany; its German settlement was a by-product of the balance between Austria, Prussia and Russia.
note.warrant: A dissolved order is replaced by whatever the victors can agree on, which is usually less than any of them wanted.
note.verdict: Sufficient, high confidence. The Empire's end made a new German frame unavoidable; the Confederation's exact form needed the Austro-Prussian-Russian balance of 1815.

note.claim: The Confederation gave Germans a frame that could neither unify nor liberalise, which turned national and liberal demands into the same demand by 1848.
note.objection: The revolutions of 1848 were continental and began in Paris; the harvest failures of 1845-47 and the French example rank with the Confederation's frustrations.
note.warrant: An order that blocks two reforms at once joins their supporters.
note.verdict: Contributing, moderate confidence. The set: the Paris revolution of February 1848 (ranks first), the subsistence crisis of 1845-47 (second), the Confederation's frustration of liberals and nationalists (third).

note.claim: The Zollverein made the German economy Prussian before the German state was, so that when unification came the question of who would lead it had been answered by trade.
note.objection: The customs union had no army; Austria could have broken it by joining or by winning in 1866, and the political union needed three wars that Bismarck chose.
note.warrant: Economic union precedes political union and decides who leads it.
note.verdict: Contributing, high confidence. The set: the wars of 1864-71 (ranks first), the Zollverein (second), the dualism (third). The Zollverein explains the leader rather than the fact of unification.

tests.hoop: Austria excluded from the union and from the Empire (passed)
tests.gun: No document shows the union decisive; Bismarck's own account credits the wars

note.claim: The Frankfurt Parliament's failure showed that unification would not come by assembly, and Bismarck's 'iron and blood' speech of 1862 is the explicit answer to 1849.
note.objection: Bismarck's unification used much of Frankfurt's work: the 1871 constitution borrowed the 1849 franchise and the Reichstag; the liberals joined him rather than being replaced.
note.warrant: A failed attempt teaches the next attempt what to avoid and leaves it the tools it built.
note.verdict: Contributing, high confidence. The set: the wars (ranks first), the Zollverein (second), Frankfurt's precedent (third).

note.claim: A new great power in the centre of Europe with no colonies joined the scramble late and convened the conference that set its rules, accelerating a partition already under way.
note.objection: Leopold's Congo and the French advance on the Niger were in motion before 1871; Bismarck disliked colonies and called the conference to manage a European quarrel rather than to acquire Africa.
note.warrant: A new power that cannot expand at home expands abroad, and its arrival changes the rules for everyone.
note.verdict: Contributing, high confidence. The set: Leopold's Congo venture (ranks first), Anglo-French rivalry on the Niger (second), German entry (third), the technologies of quinine and the Maxim gun (fourth).

note.claim: A unified Germany in the centre of Europe, industrialising faster than its neighbours and governed by a constitution that gave the army and the Kaiser the last word, made a continental war likely within two generations.
note.objection: Every great power took decisions in July 1914 that could have gone the other way, and Serbia, Austria and Russia made the first moves; the war's date was chosen in a month, whatever the pressures of the decades.
note.warrant: A structural pressure raises the base rate of war; it does not pick the year, and the year is where the dispute lies.
note.verdict: Contested, moderate confidence. One reading holds that Germany's leaders sought a war to break the encirclement they had built; the other holds that blame was shared and the outcome contingent on a month of avoidable choices. The documents support each in part, and the atlas shows both.

tests.hoop: German war planning assumed a two-front war from 1894 (passed)
tests.gun: The September Programme of 1914 shows aims, not intent before the crisis (fails as smoking gun)

note.claim: Bismarck's dismissal and the lapse of the Reinsurance Treaty three months later left Russia without a German guarantee, and Russia took the French alliance it had refused for a decade.
note.objection: Russian borrowing in Paris from 1888 was already tying the tsar to France; the alliance might have come even with Bismarck in office.
note.warrant: A guarantee withdrawn is read as a threat made.
note.verdict: Necessary, high confidence. Without the lapse, Russia had no reason to accept military obligations to France; the loans bought goodwill, the lost treaty bought the alliance.

tests.hoop: Russian approaches to France began within months of the lapse (passed)
tests.gun: Giers's correspondence names the lost treaty as the reason (passed)

note.claim: The Franco-Russian alliance gave Germany the two-front war it feared, and the Schlieffen Plan written to win it required attacking France through Belgium in any war with Russia, which brought Britain in.
note.objection: Alliances deter as well as entangle; the alliance kept peace for twenty years, and the decision to execute the plan in 1914 was Berlin's.
note.warrant: A war plan written for one scenario decides how every scenario is fought.
note.verdict: Contributing, high confidence. The set: the July decisions in Vienna, Berlin and St Petersburg (ranks first), the alliance structure (second), the naval race (third).

note.claim: Germany's battle fleet drove Britain to settle with France in 1904 and Russia in 1907, so that in 1914 Britain was aligned against Germany.
note.objection: Britain entered the war over Belgium, and the fleet race had been lost by Germany and effectively ended by 1912; the Entente had other causes, chiefly the balance on the continent.
note.warrant: A challenge to a hegemon's core interest recruits that hegemon to the challenger's enemies.
note.verdict: Contributing, moderate confidence. The set: the continental balance (ranks first), Belgium (second), the naval race (third).

note.claim: The treaty was the war's settlement: its terms follow from the war's outcome, the armistice of November 1918 and the Allies' aims.
note.objection: The treaty's particular severity, the war-guilt clause and the reparations figure were choices made in Paris, chiefly by France, and could have been different.
note.warrant: A war produces a settlement; the victors' domestic politics write its terms.
note.verdict: Sufficient, high confidence. Without the war there is no treaty; the war is enough to explain that there was one and that Germany lost, and the Paris conference explains what it said.

note.claim: The treaty's award of Germany's Shandong concessions to Japan rather than China triggered the student protests of May 4, 1919 in Beijing.
note.objection: The New Culture movement was under way from 1915; the protest's size and legacy came from that, and Shandong was the occasion.
note.warrant: A settlement that applies its principles selectively creates a grievance wherever it applied them least.
note.verdict: Contributing, high confidence. The set: the New Culture movement (ranks first), the Shandong clause (second), the warlord government's weakness (third).

note.claim: Reparations set at 132 billion gold marks in 1921 added an external debt the Weimar state could only meet by printing.
note.objection: Germany had financed the war by borrowing rather than taxing, so the mark had already lost most of its value by 1919; the 1923 collapse followed the decision to pay striking Ruhr workers with new money after the French occupation.
note.warrant: External debt destroys a currency only through the domestic decision to monetise it.
note.verdict: Contributing, high confidence. The set: war finance (necessary), the Ruhr occupation (ranks first in 1923), the printing decision (sufficient for the final phase), reparations (third). The popular chain overstates.

note.claim: Versailles handed every German party a grievance that the republic, as its signatory, could not disown, and the Nazis made revision their programme.
note.objection: Weimar survived the treaty for a decade and was stabilising by 1928; the Depression collapsed the centre, and the appointment of January 1933 was the conservatives' decision.
note.warrant: A settlement harsh enough to be hated and too lenient to disable its loser makes revision the one policy everyone can agree on.
note.verdict: Contributing, high confidence, for the appointment itself. The set: the Depression (necessary), the conservatives' co-option (ranks first among the contributors), Versailles (second), Bolshevik fear (third). The treaty's weight sits on two other arrows: it made the republic's legitimacy deficit (Necessary) and decided the revisionist content of German nationalism (Necessary). The Depression decided that Germany would break; Versailles decided what the break would look like.

note.claim: The remilitarisation of the Rhineland in March 1936 was a step in a programme whose content, the reversal of Versailles clause by clause, the treaty itself defined.
note.objection: Hitler's aims went far beyond revision, to Lebensraum in the east; the Versailles programme was the respectable cover for them.
note.warrant: A treaty's terms become the agenda of the party that promises to undo them.
note.verdict: Necessary, high confidence. The specific sequence of 1935-39, conscription, the Rhineland, Austria, the Sudetenland, is the treaty read backwards; without it the programme has a different shape and a weaker domestic consensus.

note.claim: The crash ended the short-term American lending that had financed Germany's recovery since the Dawes Plan, and the called loans carried the Depression to Germany within a year.
note.objection: German agriculture was in depression from 1927 and the economy had slowed before the crash; the credit withdrawal deepened a downturn already present.
note.warrant: An economy financed by foreign short-term credit imports the lender's crisis.
note.verdict: Necessary, high confidence. Without the withdrawal of American credit the German slowdown of 1928-29 is a recession; the 6 million unemployed of 1932 required the banking collapse that the called loans produced.

note.claim: The Depression made the Nazi party a mass movement: unemployment rose from 1.3 million in 1929 to over 6 million in 1932, and the NSDAP vote from 2.6% in 1928 to 37.3% in July 1932.
note.objection: The Nazis never won a majority and their vote fell in November 1932; Hitler was appointed by conservatives who believed they could use him. The Depression explains the vote, not the appointment.
note.warrant: An anti-system party needs a collapse of the system's output before elites will treat it as a partner.
note.verdict: Necessary, high confidence. The objection is right about the mechanism of January 1933 and wrong about the grade: without a 37% party there is nothing for Papen and Hindenburg to co-opt. Co-option is Contributing; the Depression is the precondition.

tests.gun: Papen-Hindenburg calculation that Hitler was too large to exclude, January 1933 (passed)

note.claim: The collapse of silk exports and farm incomes after 1929 strengthened the Kwantung Army's case that Japan needed Manchuria's resources and land.
note.objection: The army had planned the Manchurian seizure independently and acted without Tokyo's approval; its timetable owed more to Chinese nationalism and Soviet recovery than to the slump.
note.warrant: An economic shock does not create an expansionist faction; it removes the arguments against it.
note.verdict: Contributing, moderate confidence. The set: the Kwantung Army's autonomy (ranks first), Chinese reunification under Chiang threatening Japan's position (second), the Depression (third).

note.claim: The Bolshevik revolution gave German conservatives a fear that made an alliance with Hitler look like the lesser danger, and gave the Nazis their most effective enemy.
note.objection: The KPD's vote in 1932 was 17%, and the conservatives' fear was of the left in general; Hitler's appointment turned on Papen's intrigue and Hindenburg's exhaustion rather than on Moscow.
note.warrant: A revolution abroad arms the extremes at home by giving each a foreign example to invoke.
note.verdict: Contributing, moderate confidence. The set: the Depression (necessary), elite co-option (contributing, first among the contributors), Versailles (second), Bolshevik fear (third).

note.claim: No other German government in 1939 invades Poland; the war's timing, aims and conduct were Hitler's.
note.objection: German revisionism was consensual across parties and a conservative government would also have sought to reverse Versailles in the east, perhaps by war with Poland.
note.warrant: A regime's ideology decides which of the available wars it fights, and how.
note.verdict: Necessary, high confidence. A revisionist war over Danzig by another government is conceivable; a war of racial conquest across the continent is not. The counterfactual produces a different war or none.

tests.hoop: The decision for war in 1939 was Hitler's against his generals' advice (passed)
tests.gun: The Hossbach memorandum of 1937 records the intent (passed)

note.claim: Munich handed Hitler the Czech fortifications and arms industry without a fight and convinced him that Britain and France would not fight for Poland either.
note.objection: The war's cause was in Berlin; Munich at most set its date, and the year it bought was used by Britain to rearm, so that 1939 was a better year for the Allies than 1938 would have been.
note.warrant: Appeasement teaches the appeased what the appeaser will tolerate; it does not create the appetite.
note.verdict: Contributing, moderate confidence. The set: Hitler's intent (necessary), the Nazi-Soviet pact that removed the two-front problem (ranks first among contributors), Munich's lesson (second).

note.claim: The failure of the invasion of the Soviet Union put a Soviet army on the Elbe in 1945, and two Germanies followed from where the armies stood.
note.objection: Division was a political choice made between 1945 and 1949, and a unified neutral Germany was offered by Stalin in 1952; the armies made division possible, not inevitable.
note.warrant: The army on the ground at the ceasefire draws the border more than any treaty.
note.verdict: Necessary, high confidence. Without a Soviet army in central Germany there is no Soviet zone and no second state. The 1952 note is a real objection to Sufficient, which is why the grade is Necessary and not higher.

note.claim: Luther's 1543 tract against the Jews is cited as the root of German antisemitism and was reprinted by the Nazis.
note.objection: Anti-Jewish violence and expulsion predate Luther by centuries across Catholic Europe; Nazi racial antisemitism was a nineteenth-century pseudo-scientific doctrine that discarded the religious frame Luther used.
note.warrant: A later movement's choice of ancestor is evidence about the movement, not about the ancestor.
note.verdict: Coincident, high confidence. The Nazis used Luther as a respectable ancestor; the mechanism runs from 1870s race theory and post-1918 scapegoating. The text is evidence of continuity in prejudice rather than a cause of its 1930s form.

note.claim: The hyperinflation of 1923 is popularly held to have driven Germans to Hitler.
note.objection: The NSDAP vote fell after the 1924 stabilisation to 2.6% in 1928 and rose only with deflation and unemployment in 1930-32; the memory of 1923 mattered, but the crisis that elected Hitler was deflationary.
note.warrant: The crisis a country remembers is not always the one that decided its politics.
note.verdict: Coincident, moderate confidence. The inflation discredited the republic with the middle class and that mattered in 1930; as a cause of the vote it is the wrong decade.

note.claim: Victory over France let Bismarck proclaim the Empire in the Hall of Mirrors on January 18, 1871, with the south German states joining under the pressure of a national war.
note.objection: The south German states had treaties with Prussia from 1866 and the Zollverein from 1834; the war decided the timing and the form rather than the fact.
note.warrant: A national war is the cheapest way to make a nation agree to a state.
note.verdict: Sufficient, high confidence. The war is enough to explain the proclamation when and where it happened; the longer causes explain why the war could do it.

note.claim: The March 1848 risings forced the German princes to permit elections, and the Frankfurt assembly met in May.
note.objection: The assembly's composition and programme came from the liberal movement of the 1830s and 40s; the revolution opened the door it then walked through.
note.warrant: A revolution that frightens a ruler buys the reformers one session.
note.verdict: Sufficient, high confidence. Without the March risings the princes had refused elections for thirty years and would have gone on refusing; the revolution is enough to explain the assembly.

note.claim: The Empire's dissolution in 1806 left Germany without any frame at all, so that from Vienna onward the question was what would replace it, and every answer between 1815 and 1871 was an attempt to fill that void.
note.objection: Sixty-five years separate the two, and the Confederation of 1815 was designed to make unification impossible; the void was filled by Prussian arms, which 1806 did nothing to create.
note.warrant: A dissolved frame makes its replacement a live question for as long as none is agreed.
note.verdict: Contributing, moderate confidence. The set: the wars of 1864-71 (ranks first), the Zollverein (second), nationalism after 1813 (third), the void of 1806 (fourth).

note.claim: Hitler's regime chose the war that put a Soviet army on the Elbe, and Germany's division in 1949 followed from the occupation that war produced.
note.objection: The division was decided by the Allies between 1945 and 1949 and was offered up for reversal by Stalin in 1952; Hitler produced the occupation, and the occupiers produced the division.
note.warrant: A regime that loses a total war loses the right to decide what replaces it.
note.verdict: Necessary, high confidence. Without the Nazi state there is no war of 1939-45 in that form, no occupation and no zones; the counterfactual Germany of 1949 is unified and bordered as in 1937. The objection is right that the occupiers chose division, which is why the grade stops at Necessary.

note.claim: The division of 1949 defined reunification as the goal every West German government held in law, so that when the Soviet grip loosened in 1989 the merger was ready to be claimed within a year.
note.objection: Reunification was decided in Moscow and Washington, by Gorbachev's refusal to use force and Bush's support for Kohl; the division explains the goal and leaves its achievement to others.
note.warrant: A state that keeps a claim alive in law and institutions can act on it the moment the external veto lifts; one that has given it up cannot.
note.verdict: Contributing, high confidence. The set: Gorbachev's refusal to use force ranks first, the East German economic and legitimacy collapse of 1989 second, and the Federal Republic's standing claim to one German nation third; without the third the Soviet retreat produces two German states in a confederation, as the SPD and many East Germans proposed in late 1989.

tests.hoop: The Basic Law's reunification mandate and the Federal Republic's refusal to recognise GDR citizenship were in force in 1989 (passed)
tests.gun: None: no document shows the merger impossible without the standing claim

note.claim: The 1990 settlement embedded Germany on the assumption that Russia would be a partner and the United States the guarantor, so that when Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022 the country had neither the army nor the energy independence to respond and had to rebuild both.
note.objection: The invasion itself caused the rearmament; any German settlement would have faced the same shock, and the peace dividend was a choice of the 2000s before it was a consequence of 1990.
note.warrant: A settlement that outsources a state's security and energy to two outside powers transfers the state's future choices to those powers' conduct.
note.verdict: Contributing, moderate confidence. The set: Russia's invasion ranks first, as the sufficient trigger; the post-1990 choice of trade and gas over defence second; and the 1990 settlement's cap on German arms and its dependence on the American guarantee third, because it made the choice of the 2000s the path of least resistance.

tests.hoop: German defence spending fell from 2.5 per cent of output in 1990 to about 1.2 per cent by 2015 (passed)
tests.gun: None: no document ties the 2022 fund to the terms of 1990 directly

stories.title: The German Question
stories.sub: a country in the middle of Europe, 1517 to today
stories.thesis: Germany's position in the centre of Europe meant that every answer to how it should be organised was also an answer to how Europe should be, and from 1517 to 1990 no settlement of one question held without a settlement of the other.
assumptions: Assumes the nation-state was the destination, which the Holy Roman Empire's defenders would have denied.
Assumes the religious split of 1517 is the start; a case can be made for the Investiture Contest or for 1806.
Assumes Germany's problem was structural, position and size, before it was ideological.
stories.disconfirm: If the thesis were wrong, a German settlement imposed without a European one should have held. The Empire of 1871 is the test: it settled Germany internally and lasted 47 years before Europe unsettled it.
stories.awkward: Germany was at peace for 43 years after 1871 and the Bismarckian system managed the European side of the question better than any settlement before or since. The structural thesis has to explain the long calm as well as the collapse.

shelf.t: Iron Kingdom: The Rise and Downfall of Prussia, 1600-1947
The Thirty Years War: Europe's Tragedy
The Sleepwalkers: How Europe Went to War in 1914
Germany's Aims in the First World War
The Coming of the Third Reich
A History of Germany 1918-2014: The Divided Nation

chapters.title: The split
chapters.s1: Luther's challenge in 1517 broke the one institution that could arbitrate between German princes, and the Empire never again had an authority above its parts.
chapters.s2: The Reformation's political effect in Germany was institutional before it was theological. Once princes could choose a confession, the Emperor and the papal courts lost the standing to judge between them, and every territorial dispute acquired a religious side that made compromise a betrayal. Augsburg in 1555 ratified the stalemate rather than resolving it, and left Calvinism and secularised church lands outside its terms. The sixty-three years of peace that followed are the awkward fact for anyone who wants 1517 to lead straight to 1618; the war needed Habsburg ambition and a Bohemian election as well. What the split supplied was the frame in which a local quarrel became everyone's.

chapters.title: The settlement
chapters.s1: Thirty years of war ended in a settlement that fixed German fragmentation in law and made it a European interest to keep it so.
chapters.s2: Westphalia's German content was precise: some 300 territories gained rights of alliance and war, the Emperor's powers were bounded, and France and Sweden became guarantors with a standing interest in a weak centre. The settlement worked for 158 years, which is longer than most, and the Empire kept courts and diets that functioned. The claim that 1648 invented sovereignty is contested and the atlas grades it so; what is not contested is that from 1648 the organisation of Germany was a matter for the European powers, and that is the thesis of this arc stated in a treaty.

chapters.title: The void
chapters.s1: Napoleon ended the thousand-year frame in 1806, and for the first time Germans had to decide what Germany was.
chapters.s2: The Empire's dissolution was an act of French policy: Napoleon reorganised the German states as clients in the Confederation of the Rhine, and Francis II laid down the imperial crown in August 1806 to keep it out of Napoleon's hands. Vienna in 1815 filled the void with the German Confederation, 39 states under Austrian presidency, built to prevent both unification and liberalism. It did both for thirty years, and in doing so made nationalists and liberals the same people with the same demand. The Zollverein of 1834 answered the economic half of the question before anyone had answered the political half, and answered it in Prussia's favour.

chapters.title: Unification
chapters.s1: Prussia answered the question by force in three wars, and the answer of 1871 settled Germany while unsettling Europe.
chapters.s2: Frankfurt's failure in 1849 showed unification would not come by assembly; Bismarck's wars of 1864, 1866 and 1870 showed it would come by Prussian arms, and the Zollverein had decided in advance that Prussia rather than Austria would be the state it came under. The Empire proclaimed at Versailles was the strongest economy and army on the continent, with a constitution in which the army and the Kaiser answered to no parliament. For twenty years Bismarck's alliances kept France isolated and Europe calm, which is the awkward fact for the structural thesis. The calm ended with his dismissal in 1890 and the lapse of the Russian treaty, after which Germany faced the two-front alliance it had been built to prevent.

chapters.title: The war
chapters.s1: Whether the Empire of 1871 made 1914 likely is the central live argument about the war, and the atlas holds it open.
chapters.s2: One reading holds that Germany's position and its leaders' aims made a continental war a matter of time; the other holds that July 1914 was a crisis in which every power took decisions that could have gone otherwise, with Vienna and St Petersburg moving first. The documents support each in part. What is settled is the mechanism of the alliances: the Franco-Russian treaty of 1894 gave Germany a two-front war, the Schlieffen Plan written to win it required attacking France through Belgium in any war with Russia, and Belgium brought Britain in. A structural pressure raised the base rate of war; the year was chosen in a July.

chapters.title: The treaty
chapters.s1: Versailles settled the war on terms harsh enough to be hated and too lenient to disable the loser, and revision became the one policy every German party agreed on.
chapters.s2: The treaty took 13% of Germany's territory, assigned guilt in Article 231 and set reparations at 132 billion gold marks in 1921. Its design flaw, named by Foch at the time, was the gap between its severity and its enforcement. The republic that signed it could never fully own the state, and the treaty's clauses became the programme of whoever promised to undo them. Two popular chains are graded down here: reparations ranks third among the causes of the 1923 inflation, behind war finance and the Ruhr; and the treaty ranks third among the causes of Hitler's appointment, behind the Depression and the conservatives' miscalculation. Its weight is elsewhere: it decided what a German collapse would look like when one came.

chapters.title: The collapse
chapters.s1: Weimar was stabilising by 1928; the Depression broke it, and the conservatives who thought they could use Hitler handed him the state.
chapters.s2: German recovery after 1924 ran on short-term American credit, and the crash called it in. Unemployment rose from 1.3 million to 6 million, Brüning governed by decree and deflated to defend the currency, and the NSDAP vote went from 2.6% in 1928 to 37.3% in July 1932. The Nazis never won a majority and their vote fell in November 1932; Hitler was appointed in January 1933 by Papen and Hindenburg, who calculated that a party of that size could be used and could not be excluded. The Depression is graded Necessary: without a 37% party there was nothing to co-opt. The hyperinflation of 1923 is graded Coincident: the crisis that elected Hitler was deflationary, a decade later.

chapters.title: The division
chapters.s1: Hitler's war ended with a Soviet army on the Elbe, and two Germanies followed from where the armies stood.
chapters.s2: No other German government invades Poland in 1939, and no other fights the war Hitler fought in the east. The invasion of the Soviet Union failed, the Red Army reached the Elbe in April 1945, and the occupation zones became states in 1949. Division was a choice made between 1945 and 1949, and Stalin's note of 1952 offering a neutral united Germany is the objection that keeps the grade at Necessary rather than Sufficient. The German question had its answer imposed from outside for forty-one years, which is the thesis in its starkest form: Europe settled Germany because Germany could not be allowed to settle itself.

chapters.title: The reunification
chapters.s1: The Soviet retreat of 1989 let the two Germanies merge in 1990 on terms four outside powers set: inside NATO, inside the European Community, and soon without its own currency.
chapters.s2: Kohl's ten-point plan of November 1989 and the Two Plus Four treaty of September 1990 settled the German question by embedding the enlarged state: NATO membership kept the United States in Europe as a guarantor, the Maastricht treaty of 1992 traded the Deutsche Mark for the euro as the price of French consent, and the army was capped at 370,000. The settlement rested on two assumptions the next thirty years tested: that Russia would stay a partner, and that the United States would stay the guarantor.

chapters.title: The rearmament
chapters.s1: Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022 broke both assumptions of 1990 at once, and Germany answered with the largest rearmament in Europe since 1945, which reopens the old question in a new form.
chapters.s2: The Zeitenwende fund of 2022, the debt-brake amendment of 2025 and the NATO target of 3.5 per cent by 2035 commit Germany to a conventional army larger than any other in western Europe. The question of 1871, what a strong Germany in the middle of Europe means for its neighbours, returns with the signs reversed: Poland and the Baltic states now ask Berlin to be stronger, France asks it to be stronger inside European structures, and the German public is unsure it wants the role. The settlement of 1990 held because Germany was embedded and unarmed; the next settlement has to hold with Germany embedded and armed.

stories.today: The question is open again. Germany committed in 2025 to 3.5 per cent of output on defence by 2035 and amended its constitution to pay for it; the army it is building will be the largest in western Europe. Watch three things: whether the spending survives a change of government and a recession, whether Poland and France can agree on what a strong Germany is for, and whether the United States stays the guarantor the 1990 settlement assumed.

themes.title: Man and Power
themes.passage: Every society must decide who commands and persuade the rest to obey, and the persuading has always been the harder part. Kings pointed to God, republics to the people, dictators to the emergency; each claim held exactly as long as it was believed, and belief has failed before fear every time. Power is cheap to seize and expensive to keep, and the price is paid in legitimacy, a currency no regime has ever been able to print.
themes.covers: consent, inheritance, charisma, force; democracy and despotism as traffic between them; revolution

themes.title: Man and God
tension: the sacred as the state's foundation
themes.passage: Faith has built more states than it has broken and broken only those that tried to own it. Men have killed for a doctrine, died for it, and then, exhausted, learned to tolerate what they could not convert; the toleration came from fatigue first and philosophy later. Every century since has announced the end of religion in politics, and religion has not read the announcement.
themes.covers: Reformation, toleration, holy war, secularisation, religion's return to politics

themes.title: Man and War
themes.passage: War is the oldest of institutions and the one most often pronounced dead. Men fight, as Thucydides wrote, out of fear, honour and interest, and the balance among the three decides whether the war is short or ruinous. The peace that follows is the most consequential act of any war, and it is almost always made by men too tired to make it well.
themes.covers: the international system, alliances, deterrence, settlements

themes.title: Man and Scarcity
themes.passage: There has never been enough, and every economic system is a proposal about who should go without. Markets, plans, guilds, empires and rationing are all answers to the same arithmetic, and each has starved someone. The discovery of the modern age is the darkest one: that men die of hunger beside full granaries when no one is permitted to say that they are dying.
themes.covers: famine amid plenty, capitalism and its rivals, debt, one commodity becoming a nation's politics

themes.title: Man and Machine
themes.passage: Man makes his tools, and then his tools make the world he must live in. Print made the Reformation possible and the nation-state inevitable; steam built the factory, the city and the colony; the bomb gave the great powers a peace founded on terror; the network has assembled a crowd that never goes home. Every machine has arrived as a servant, and none has stayed one.
themes.covers: print, steam, the bomb, the network

cases.case: the Green Revolution's defeat of famine

themes.title: Man and Nature
themes.passage: Climate, plague and distance governed human affairs long before anyone thought to record it, and they govern still. The crops and pathogens that crossed the Atlantic after 1492 moved more people and killed more than any conqueror in history. Nature is the slowest actor on the stage and the one that is always still there when the others have left.
themes.covers: the Columbian exchange, plague, the little ice age, coal, the warming century

themes.title: Man and the Stranger
themes.passage: Every people has drawn a line between itself and the others, by blood, faith, tongue, colour or paper, and the line has been redrawn more often by lawyers than by soldiers. Who may belong decides who may own, vote, move, marry and live. The twentieth century widened the circle further than any age before it and, in the same decades, closed it with a thoroughness no age had managed.

themes.title: Man and Truth
themes.passage: Every age has appointed a keeper of truth, church, crown, academy or press, and every age has lived through the day the keeper lost the keys. Gutenberg, Galileo, Darwin and the algorithm each broke a monopoly on what may be known, and in every case the breaking shook the state more than the knowledge did. Who is permitted to say a thing is true has mattered as much as whether it is.
themes.covers: Galileo, the press, Darwin, propaganda, the laboratory, the feed

themes.title: Man and Time
themes.passage: Men have believed that history climbs, that it falls, and that it turns in a circle, and each belief has fitted the facts for about a century before the facts moved. Whether history is going anywhere is the question beneath all the others in this atlas, and the atlas leaves it open, showing which claims about the direction of things have survived five hundred years of evidence and which have failed.
themes.covers: Ibn Khaldun's dynasties, the Enlightenment's arrow, the twentieth century's doubt

themes.title: Man and Memory
themes.passage: A people is made by what it chooses to remember and unmade by what it cannot forget. Nations build more monuments to their defeats than to their victories, because a defeat can be owned by everyone; and how a country tells the story of its worst day is the most reliable guide to what it will do on its next one.
themes.covers: monuments and their removal, the Lost Cause, Nanjing, the Holocaust, the Nakba, chosen ancestors
